reply.sources_show: The held sources mainly list types of intervention (teacher training, ramps, assistive devices) as ways the goal 'can be achieved', with just one cited case reporting 'increased enrolment for children with disabilities'; they report no measured outcomes from a systematic review and no ranking of programme types.

sources_show_quote.quote: This led to improvements in inclusive education practice by service-providers, better physical accessibility for learners, increased enrolment for children with disabilities and a better learning environment for all students (Murenzi and Mebratu, 2013).

direction_quote.quote: Initiatives aimed at improving the quality of inclusive or specialist primary education;

reply.direction_why: The sources treat specialist as well as inclusive settings as legitimate routes, and they urge approaches that 'do not necessarily demand extra funding', so the belief that special schools are outdated and that money is the main barrier is only partly supported, though one case does show enrolment gains from accessibility and practice improvements.

kill_quote.quote: Interventions to support the enrolment of people with disabilities in formal education (inclusive or specialist)

reply.kill_note: The passages give intervention typologies and a single anecdotal case, not systematic-review evidence of consistent, well-measured gains or a ranking of programme types, so the kill condition is not met.
